Skip next section CDU slips under 5% parliament threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — projections

CDU slips under 5% parliament threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — projections

Germany's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will not enter the next parliament in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to projections published by Germany's top public broadcasters.

The latest predictions published by public broadcaster ARD put the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz at 4.9%, cementing its worst-ever defeat in a state election of this kind. Another German public broadcaster, ZDF, initially maintained its 5% projection before also adjusting its estimates to 4.9%.

The conservative party is not the only one in danger of falling below the legal limit, with the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknech Alliance (BSW) also seemingly just below the threshold.

If both of these factions are kept out of the next parliament, the new assembly would have only four parties: the far-right AfD, the center-left SPD, the socialist Left Party, and the environmentally friendly Greens.

The AfD would still require a coalition partner to form a majority.

Skip next section CDU faces its worst-ever state election defeat in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

CDU faces its worst-ever state election defeat in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is fighting to stay in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament, with its result hovering around the 5% mark. 

However, even if the conservatives are represented in the next state parliament, the Sunday election already marks their worst ever election defeat in the state parliamentary votes held anywhere in Germany. The party, founded in 1945, was traditionally considered one of the country's "big tent" political factions seeking to accommodate a wide spectrum of voters.

Its previous worst score was 9% of the vote they secured in Bremen in 1951, according to a report published by NDR, the public broadcaster covering Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Skip next section How did Berlin's young people vote?

How did Berlin's young people vote?

German citizens in Berlin aged 16 and 17 were able to cast their ballots in the state election for the first time on Sunday — and they were among a group that voted overwhelmingly for progressive parties.

According to results on Sunday evening, some 43% of voters aged 16-24 voted for the socialist Left Party. Another 12% voted for the Greens, while 7% voted for the Social Democrats (SPD).

Meanwhile, around 12% of voters aged 16-24 for the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD).

It was voters in the 25 to 34 age group who were the biggest bloc to have supported the Left Party, with 48% casting their ballots for the far-left party.

Support for the Left Party dims as the age groups grow older, with voters around 33% of voters above 70 having voted for the incumbent Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Skip next section Berlin bishops say city voted for democracy, diversity

Berlin bishops say city voted for democracy, diversity

Commenting on the Berlin state election, the city's Protestant Bishop Christian Stäblein said the majority of the voters endorsed "liberal democracy."

"We are a church bound by the Christian view of humanity and by the dignity of every person," he said.

His Catholic colleague, Heiner Koch, said his church would "continue to critically observe politics, and warn against the supposedly easy solutions, and speak up for those, who are insufficiently seen or heard in the political debate."

Berlin "is and stays diverse," the Catholic bishop said.

Skip next section Verdi chief urges Merz to rethink reforms

Verdi chief urges Merz to rethink reforms

The head of Germany's Verditrade union has called on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government to change course on planned reforms following the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

"I hope Mr Merz realizes that he has screwed up," Verdi chairman Frank Werneke told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.

Werneke called on the government to abandon plans requiring employees to provide a doctor's note from the first day of illness and ending full retirement benefits after 45 years of contributions.

"Many people reject abolishing the full pension after 45 years of contributions. That is an important reason for the CDU's poor performance in the recent elections," Werneke said. "People are worn out and exhausted. They want to stop working, and they need to."

Werneke also described the recent electoral gains of the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) as "extremely threatening."

"An AfD federal government would be a catastrophe," he said, arguing that leaving the euro and European Union would be economically disastrous and that Germany needed immigration.

"Everything must be done to ensure that the AfD does not enter government," Werneke said.

Verdi and other trade unions plan a nationwide day of protest on Saturday, with demonstrations expected in 15 cities.

Skip next section Berlin: SPD's Krach refuses to discuss new coalitions

Berlin: SPD's Krach refuses to discuss new coalitions

The top candidate for the center-left SPD in Berlin, Steffen Krach, refused to discuss cooperation with other parties in the city's Senate.

"It's too early to talk about coalition options," he said, when asked if his party would prefer to rule with the Left Party or the CDU conservatives.

Talking to state broadcaster ARD, Krach noted that the incumbent CDU-SPD coalition was clearly defeated at the polls, and that future steps will be decided within the party committees in the following weeks.

Meanwhile, the Green party indicated they were ready to rule together with the Left Party and the SPD.

"We want to take responsibility and forge a progressive alliance for Berlin together with the SPD and the Left," said senior Green representatives Nina Stahr and Philmon Ghirmai, saying that Berliners voted in favor of political change.

Skip next section Populist BSW projected to fall short, stay out of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament

Populist BSW projected to fall short, stay out of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament

According to incomplete projections published by German media, the leftist populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will not be entering the state legislature of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, depriving them of the kingmaker role they had previously secured in Saxony-Anhalt.

The estimates published by German state broadcasters ARD and ZDF just after 8 p.m. on Sunday show BSW at 4.9% of the votes, just shy of the 5% threshold they need to secure in order to be represented in the state parliament.

Moreover, the latest available numbers show Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) hovering around 5%, also putting it at risk of not having a parliamentary presence. A failure by the center-right CDU to enter the chamber would ramp up pressure on the chancellor, whose power is already shaken by the Saxony-Anhalt vote and his party's already staggeringly low result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The numbers are subject to change as the official count continues.

Skip next section Populist BSW rejects AfD coalition in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

Populist BSW rejects AfD coalition in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

With the far-right populist AfD leading the pack in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but still projected to fall well short of the parliamentary majority, the leftist populist BSW rejected the possibility of officially joining forces.

BSW's top candidate Peter Schabbel said there would be no coalition with the AfD.

"We are sticking to it," he said.

However, he noted that cooperation between the two parties was still possible, including voting together.

This language reflects BSW's attitude following the Saxony-Anhalt election two weeks ago. With the AfD also falling short of a parliamentary majority in this German state, the BSW said it would "decide on the substance" when it comes to supporting them in parliament.

On Sunday, Schabbel also sought to dispel doubts that BSW would clear the 5% hurdle to enter the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania parliament, despite the projections showing them at the very edge of the required percentage of the vote.

"We are very confident that we will get into the state assembly," Schabbel said.

Skip next section Leading CDU figure blames party firewall critics for voter uncertainty

Leading CDU figure blames party firewall critics for voter uncertainty

Senior Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician Philipp Amthor has blamed members of his own party who questioned its firewall against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) for contributing to the CDU's poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Amthor, a minister of state in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Chancellery, told public broadcaster ZDF that there was a "very clear position" across the state CDU on maintaining its distance from the AfD.

He said individual party figures had tried to soften that position, but that this had instead contributed to "even greater uncertainty among our voters here in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania."

"I am very grateful that everyone kept their nerve and did not draw the wrong conclusions," Amthor, who himself hails from the state, said.

The CDU is hovering around the 5% threshold in the latest projections, a big drop from the 13.3% it won in 2021.

Amthor described the CDU's result as a "historic defeat" and a "tectonic shift" for a party that governed Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania from 1990 to 1998.

Skip next section SPD leaders call for change after election results

SPD leaders call for change after election results

Vice Chancellor and Social Democratic Party (SPD) co-leader Lars Klingbeil has said the federal government must reassess its approach following the election results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

"We as a federal government need to analyze why there is such great uncertainty in the country," Klingbeil told public broadcaster ARD.

He said the government had failed to communicate its reforms in a way that convinced people they would bring improvements, while public debate had too often focused on spending cuts.

Klingbeil, who is also Germany's finance minister, said people's concerns over the controversial proposal to abolish full retirement benefits after 45 years of contributions needed to be taken seriously. "We will find solutions for that," he said.

SPD General Secretary Tim Klüssendorf separately called for a change of course by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU-SPD coalition.

The elections were "a very clear message that you can't simply bulldoze ahead and carry on as before," Klüssendorf told public broadcaster ZDF.

He said the government needed to make corrections, arguing that reforms should focus on structural changes rather than cuts alone.

Skip next section Berlin: 1 in 4 voters supports Left Party

Berlin: 1 in 4 voters supports Left Party

The socialist Left Party is projected to secure over 25% of the vote in the Sunday polls in the German capital, giving it 43 lawmakers in Berlin's state parliament of 159 seats.

According to latest official projections, based on partial results, Chancellor Merz's CDU expected to take just under 20% and 34 seats, with the far-right AfD in third place, with 15.6% and 27 seats in the famously liberal city.

The Green Party is less than one percentage point and one seat behind the AfD, expecting to field 26 lawmakers in the city-state legislature.

AfD maintains thin lead in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

Meanwhile, in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the AfD is still ahead of the center-left SPD, with 37.3% of the vote for the anti-immigration faction compared to 35.5% for the moderate leftists.

The Left Party is third with 7.5% of the vote in the state.

The current projections give the AfD 28 state lawmakers compared to SPD's 26, but still not enough for a ruling majority in the 71-seat state assembly.

The embedded charts will be automatically updated with the latest available results throughout the evening.

Skip next section Germany's main Jewish organization 'deeply unsettled' by Left Party victory in Berlin

Germany's main Jewish organization 'deeply unsettled' by Left Party victory in Berlin

The Central Council of Jews in Germany, the country's main Jewish organization, has criticized the Left Party's election win in Berlin.

"That a party whose campaign openly called for the death of people has emerged victorious from the election deeply disturbs me," said Josef Schuster, the president of the organization.

Schuster accused the Left Party of having crossed the line into antisemitism in a statement, saying that the party openly called for an intifada (which translates to "uprising") and the death of Israeli soldiers during campaign season. 

He was referring to a campaign event where a rapper addressing the crowd called out "Death to the IDF," referring to the Israeli military. The Left Party mayoral candidate Elif Eralp condemned the performance and promised an internal investigation.

Eralp also said that she firmly stood "for the protection of Jewish life and against all forms of antisemitism."

Schuster added in his statement: "To this day, there have been no personnel or political consequences."

He called on the center-left SPD and the Greens to prevent the Left Party from participating in the Berlin city government.

The Central Council of Jews in Germany has also criticized the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD), calling it "a party where antisemites and far-right extremists have found a home."

Sunday's election in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania took place in ​a period of heightened anxiety ⁠for many Jewish people in Europe, where there has been a sharp rise in antisemitic attacks and incidents since the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent Israeli campaign in Gaza.

Skip next section WATCH: Chancellor Merz defiant after state election defeats

WATCH: Chancellor Merz defiant after state election defeats

Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany needed "reforms" and pledged to "get down to business" of reshaping the country despite mounting pressure on his party.

Skip next section Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania incumbent achieves comeback, but falls short of hopes

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania incumbent achieves comeback, but falls short of hopes

It is not a bad result for the center-left Social Democrats, who have been in power in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania for 28 years. In fact, it was a huge comeback that very few expected only a few months ago.

But it was also clear here that there was some disappointment for not having managed to snatch that first place from the far-right AfD. The room remained very quiet as the first exit polls were read out. Only at the end did a long applause break out.

Real enthusiasm came only when state premier and lead candidate Manuela Schwesig took the stage. "Manu, Manu" chants and clapping filled the room.

It's clear how beloved she is here — she is the main and possibly only reason the Social Democrats were able to get into a neck-and-neck race with the AfD.

Skip next section Weidel calls on CDU to drop firewall against AfD

Weidel calls on CDU to drop firewall against AfD

Speaking in Berlin, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel has called on the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to end its firewall against cooperation with her party.

Weidel told public broadcaster ZDF that the CDU was weak partly because it refused to work with the AfD.

"Voters have consistently been voting center-right," she said, arguing that the CDU could have formed governments with the AfD at both state and federal level.

Weidel said voters wanted a change of political direction and that Chancellor Friedrich Merz should draw the consequences from the election results.

"Our goal is, of course, to hold coalition talks with the CDU in the long term, but we will under no circumstances compromise our positions," she said.
